utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Tieger, are you ready to condition the examination-in-chief of Witness Tupajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then when awaiting the arrival of the witness in the courtroom - Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom - I would like to address two matters briefly. One is that in view of Witness 606 there was the issue of whether the Defence objected against one statement or two statements; that has not yet been clarified where the Chamber has asked further clarification from the parties, so we would like to receive that. And then there is another matter - and that is I'm addressing you - Mr. Krajisnik, you did invite write two letters when you were invited to draft a kind of an agenda for a meeting. The Chamber would like to know whether you would like to have these letters filed so that they are part of this case. Yes, if you could tell us now, fine; if you will say, I'll tell you one of these days, it's fine as well. It's not an urgent matter, but we have to know whether or not these letters should be filed officially because they were addressed to the Judges personally.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to consult with my lawyers, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine. Then we'll hear from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony yesterday, and I would also very much ask you to answer the questions as they are put to you. So please carefully listen and address the matters that are raised in the question. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Tieger: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, just before we adjourned yesterday I had asked whether Muslim villages were shelled and burned down by the 2nd Romanija Brigade during the summer of 1992 and asked you to identify those villages, and you indicated that those activities started in Donje Babine village, and you provided some description and named some villages just before we adjourned. After the operations -- the operation in Babine village, did the 2nd Romanija Brigade then move on to conduct operations against other Muslim villages in the Sokolac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in addition to the villages you mentioned yesterday, which included Sasevci, Pitlice, Pridvorica, Grabenice, Islica -- Islica, Brdov, Kaljina and Sahbegovic, did those operations also include Ivazovici and Mangurici.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me, I would like to correct the names of the villages. The first one is Sasevci, Pridvorica, Iseric Brdo, Sahbegovici, Kaljina, with a few hamlets. This also applies to the village of Mangurici and Ivazovici, the ones that you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those villages destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how was that done? Were they first shelled by artillery? Were -- did the infantry first enter? How was that destruction accomplished?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was first artillery fire and after that and probably after the Muslim population or possibly soldiers had withdrawn, the infantry entered the villages and later on the villages were burned. We forgot to mention a big village between Knezina and Kaljina, and that is the village of Meljine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday in response to questions by Judge Hanoteau, you testified about the unlawful arrests and detentions of Muslim civilians without lawful grounds. Can you identify some of the places in which those Muslim civilians were held?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the first place where they were detained was the cellar of the primary school in Sokolac. The next one was the earlier abandoned school building in Cavarine village; and later on some of the rooms in the factory in Palez, which is a hamlet near Knezina; and finally, in a restaurant in Knezina and in the cellar of the building where the post office was and where the seat of the local commune was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what can you tell us about conditions in those detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the conditions were rather bad as far as I know. When we're talking about the cellar of the primary school, I know that in 1991 after the facilities of the football club had burned down, we used the cellar for -- as the changing rooms for the footballers. And I know that in 1991 the conditions there were bad and I believe that they were even worse in 1992. And I believe that the situation was the same in other facilities. There were no conditions to provide for even the minimum conditions for the stay of these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, whenever the witness says "I believe," as it reflects I wonder why he believes that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, as the Court noted, you stated that you believed that the conditions were rather bad, as far as you know. Then you described what you knew about the conditions in the cellar of the primary school where Muslims were held and stated that you believe that -- that you were familiar with the conditions in 1991, believed that they were even worse in 1992, and believed that the situation was the same in other facilities. Can you assist the Court in understanding the basis for your belief, both that the conditions in the cellar of the primary school were worse in 1992 than when you were familiar with them in 1991 and also why you believed that the situation was the same in other facilities.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've told you, we used those premises in 1991 for a very short stay of the footballers. They used those premises as their changing rooms. We managed to install one or two showers for the footballers to take a shower after the training. As far as I remember, there was very little light. I suppose, although I didn't have an occasion to see that, that later on the conditions deteriorated. Nobody ever used those premises. The school in Cavarine had been abandoned for years; it did not have any facilities or installations, any sewage or water pipes on the account of the period when it was constructed. As for the restaurant in Knezina, there was only one WC; this is a restaurant that had been open for years. And as for the cellar in the building where the post office and the local commune were, I didn't enter the cellars, but I know that they hadn't been used for years; they had been abandoned. And this is the basis for my belief that the conditions were rather bad. I did not see any of them, myself, but I have grounds to believe that the conditions were bad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask one additional question. You never heard about any renovation or -- of these facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under the circumstances existing at that time, would you -- would you have known if any such money and time-consuming renovations would have taken place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could only learn that somebody from the command asked for the supply of the building material for the renovation of these facilities. As far as I can remember, nobody approached us in the municipality, and that is why I'm saying that I don't have any information that any renovation of these facilities had been carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago I asked you about the operations by the 2nd Romanija Brigade against Muslim villages. Did the police also participate in those operations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any information that the police participated in such operations. No such information ever reached me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether special units of the police --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Perhaps it's best if I follow up with this question, Your Honour, before you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, do you know whether special units of the police were formed during the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the territory of the municipality, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I am --

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question fully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in particular with an interest in the forces that participated in operations against municipality villages, I wanted to know if you were aware of or had any information on the establishment of special units of the police that might have cooperated with or worked with or engaged in operations with the 2nd Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, neither the regular police from the public security station nor the special police participated in that. Because the 2nd Romanija Brigade was very strong, had a lot of troops, and I believed that they did not need any assistance in those operations. In Sokolac there was never any special police unit. Special police was established in other areas. However, there were a number of military conscripts that were assigned to some units of the special police; I don't know how many. I know that for a while the headquarters of one of those units was on Mount Jahorina as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't know if you wanted to follow up at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise for having interrupted you at the moment when you were asking your questions. I would like to follow up on what the witness has said. He has told us -- [In English] "There was first artillery fire and after that, probably after the Muslim population or possibly soldiers had withdrawn, the infantry entered the villages." [Interpretation] It seems that first there was artillery fire, according to what the witness has told us, and then the population withdrew and -- the possible soldiers, and then the infantry would enter the villages in order to set fire to the houses. Is that what you've told us? Is that how you've described the events to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was the case. As far as I remember, we discussed that yesterday already. I would like to say that the women, children, and the elderly, according to the information that we had at the time, even before that, as soon as there were first actions in Babine village, they started withdrawing towards Olovo. At the moment there was shelling, I don't think that there were any civilians, and I'm primarily referring to the women, children, and the elderly in the village. According to my information, there were no casualties among the civilian population, so you have understood my answer properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, I wonder if you might clarify something for me, and in connection with that I wanted to turn to the interview of November 13th at page 25. This was an interview involving you and representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor in -- on November 13th of 2003. And at page 25 you were asked: "What role did the Serbian police in Sokolac play in supporting the military operations against the Muslim villages in July, August, and September of 1992?" And your answer, at least as it was recorded here, was: "As far as I know, the police was organised along the line of the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, and they formed special units that they deployed to help the army. I remember a visit that I made when they were on the Nisic plateau. They were deployed on the Nisic plateau. The deployment of these units was probably coordinated between the people from the Main Staff, but in 1992 most of the policemen were used in the battlefields." I was wondering if you could help us in reconciling that with your previous answer about the -- to the question about use of special units of the police.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, my visit to the Nisic plateau and the visit to the policemen who were on the strength of that unit did not happen in 1992. That was later on. I don't know whether it was in 1993 or 1994. There is nothing disputable about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the question, as it was posed in the interview, focussed on the military operations in the summer of 1992. And in your answer, again according to the transcript, you concluded by saying: "In 1992, most of the policemen were used in the battlefields." Do I understand you correctly that you say that you either didn't mean 1992 or that the transcript incorrectly reflected your answer that it was on -- during some year other than 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this direction, the direction of Olovo where the 2nd Romanija Brigade was active, was only one of the directions and one of the locations where the members of the then 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade were deployed. The police, and quite a few of them from the police station in fact, as far as I can remember, were busy in Sarajevo. I believe that in the summer and autumn in 1992 they were near the Jewish cemetery within the framework of the unit which was set up by the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, the question put to you during the interview as we read it was not only about July, August, and September of 1992, but also mentioned military operations against the Muslim villages and the involvement of the police in that. If you say it was at a later stage, do you mean to say that operations against Muslim villages were -- took place later than in July, August, and September 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The activities that started in the village of Babine -- well, it was in the beginning of August/end of July. And that was the start of the operations that we had referred to before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That continued until when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think already by the end of September the demarcation line was set up along the villages of Krusevo, Dugandzici. I don't really know where exactly this demarcation line ran in the direction of the municipality of Radnik. And those lines basically remained unchanged or they were only slightly shifted until the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Part of your answer in that interview was that "These special units were deployed to help the army." To help the army with what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, I can't deny coordinating activities of the units of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska and the police units. As to the use of those units, well, it was probably a joint decision between the Main Staff and the Ministry of the Interior, that is to say the government. As to the insight of those planned operations and joined operations -- well, it's something that I myself obviously never had, but I know where police officers from Sokolac spent time at certain periods of time. One of those periods of time referred to their stay at Nisic plateau in 1992 and then the Jewish cemetery in the area of Sarajevo in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was focussing on whether such coordination took also place in relation to the operations against Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said before, I think that when it comes to these particular activities, when those villages were being taken, as far as I know there was no need for that, since there was almost no resistance to speak of as far as I know and there were no major clashes in the course of that operation. I suppose that the need arose if, that is, the need had risen, we would have asked -- or they would have asked for the help of the Ministry of the Interior, but there was no need for that because the 2nd Romanija had sufficient strength.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, I'd like to ask you another question focussed on the conditions that existed for Muslims in Sokolac municipality in the summer of 1992. In that connection, let me ask you whether members of your family hid Muslims from VRS troops during that period?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I referred to that. My parents who lived at Knezina and their next-door neighbours who were Muslims had considerable difficulties with the members of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska and especially at that time when all Muslim inhabitants, except for two infirm old women left Knezina. And during the night they sought refuge at our house and at the house of my uncle, just to spend the night because they were harassed during the day and they feared for their safety during the night, they feared the worst. Presumably they were following the events there, and on a number of occasions there was a lot of verbal abuse. I mean, my parents suffered that verbal abuse at the hands of the members of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these two elderly Muslim women the last remaining people from their village?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what eventually happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, after two months I believe, my brother managed to have them taken to the village of Burate during the night, which is a border village between the municipalities of Sokolac and Rogatica, and it was within the area of Rogatica where Muslims were still present. And afterwards they went to Sarajevo with the other Muslims, and they were safe there because they had their relatives in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like the next exhibit to be placed before the witness. As the Court is aware, there is a small packet of exhibits. I believe everyone has that other than the witness at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, logistics are improving. A telegram?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm directing everyone's attention to the telegram contained behind tab 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, just to explain, as I think you can already see, behind each tab is an English and B/C/S version of the exhibit in question. I've directed your attention to tab 1 and of course to the -- in your case to the B/C/S version of that. Can you tell us what that document is, please? And, I'm sorry, before you do so --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Perhaps I could have that marked at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be, Your Honours, P842, and the English translation 842.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, can you tell us about this telegram?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a telegram, as far as I know, which came from the then-president of the Republika Srpska, Mr. Karadzic, in the month of July. I can't remember which day exactly, but perhaps you can tell on the basis of my reply. And presumably -- well, at the time I thought it had been sent to some other or maybe all the other municipalities in the Republic of Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. And later on, a couple of days later, I saw that -- the telegram of the same content was sent to seven or eight municipalities in Eastern Bosnia. In this document the entire responsibility for any offence taking place on the territory of those municipalities is being shifted on to us as the presidents of municipalities. I was rather surprised by this telegram, since I knew that Mr. Karadzic knew full well about the way in which the system was functioning, about the way in which it was organised. I mean the system of government in the then-Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, who had what competencies, and who was in command over what forces, and who, if they wished to do so, could realistically implement the measures that he's asking us to implement in this telegram.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at two additional documents. First, very quickly, the document behind tab 2 which is previously marked and admitted Exhibit P690. Mr. Tupajic, this appears to reflect the content of the telegram and the date, also indicating that it has been sent to a number of municipalities in the following manner, including to Sokolac on the teleprinter. It indicates the date and time that the last message was sent as July 14th, at 1530 hours. It's signed by Colonel Kotlica, and it adds a PS, "I suggest that you inform the media." Did Sokolac receive the -- its information via teleprinter, as indicated in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely that. I did say early Sokolac, compared to all these other municipalities and the entire region, had the best equip -- with all the equipment, and that was the reason the telegram was actually sent to Sokolac, precisely because of that infrastructure. And then through the military services, this same telegram was forwarded to all the other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you referred to a reply in your earlier answer. Could I ask you now to turn to tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can I have that marked as the next exhibit in order, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That, Your Honours, will be P843, with the translation 843.1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, is 843 your reply to the telegram that was sent to you by Dr. Karadzic on July 14th, 1992, and was that dated -- was that sent on July 15th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we might have forgotten to give a number to the previous tab 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's P690, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, that's already in evidence. Yes, you're right, you're perfectly right. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you respond to Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic's telegram and what were you trying to tell him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, basically the gist of my reply to Mr. Karadzic is simply reminding him of the fact that I myself as the president of the municipality and the Crisis Staff, which was basically winding things up there in as far as the war was concerned, when it came to implementing his orders that we had no competence and no possibility to do so. I simply reminded him of the fact that officially the TO staff was no longer in existence since the 1st of May when the 2nd Romanija Brigade was set up and that the police stations and the chief of police which -- or rather, who in the meantime had resigned was accountable according to the line of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. command to the Ministry of the Interior. And that, quite simply, when it came to both implementing these measures at the municipal level - and I did say that we had not started with that, I mean expressing loyalty by surrendering arms - I said that we had no influence, no competence, and we could not do anything whatsoever to protect the population or guarantee their safety. I believe that -- even at the time and even now when I look back, I think it was a slightly unique and considering the circumstances at the time a rather brave answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, in the response to Dr. Karadzic, you state that the: "Activities on the area of the municipality are conducted by the station of public security and by the 2nd Romanija Brigade." That's correct, right? That's in the first paragraph of your response. And I'm referring specifically to --

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here -- well, the last sentence reads that all activities on the territory of the municipality, considering safety, were to be implemented by the command of the 2nd Romanija Brigade and the police force and that it was being done without my knowledge and the knowledge of my closest collaborators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your earlier answer about the telegram, you testified that the entire responsibility was being shifted in asserting that you would be responsible for security. Who -- or which body within Republika Srpska was ultimately in charge of the military, of the 2nd Romanija Brigade, all the way up through its chain of command, and who was at the top of the chain of command of the military in Republika Srpska in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The supreme commander of the armed forces that were made up of both the Ministry of the Interior and the military was the president of the republic; the 2nd Romanija Brigade, as a military formation; and all the other military formations, according to the hierarchy, were accountable to the corps commands. And the corps commands and their part were accountable to the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska, and they again were accountable to the president of the republic for whatever they did. And if we think about the line of command in -- within the Ministry of the Interior, and I mentioned that yesterday, the police stations were carrying out their tasks according to the instructions from the central offices of the police and they got their tasks assigned by the Minister of the Interior, the Ministry of the Interior, and the minister. I don't know whether the supreme defence council existed; it did by the end of the war, and it was made up by the most high-ranking people, especially in the area of security and military. And in my opinion, as is the case in any other country, they should have looked into all these matters and adopt an attitude or reach a decision and then issue orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Insofar as you were area in 1992, was the Minister of the Interior superior to or subordinate to the Presidency of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was subordinated to the president of the Republic of Srpska. Not just to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago you stated that you thought under the circumstances your response was a brave one. Did that have to do with that aspect of your response in telling Dr. Karadzic that you weren't responsible for the safety, he was as president or president of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The gist of my answer was precisely that. I reminded him of the system which had been set up and should have been functioning. And so at the top of the pyramid was the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you also trying to indicate in any way that there was a basis for concern about the security of -- and safety of Muslims in Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that Mr. Karadzic had the information concerning all the events up until that stage and some of the municipalities that received those telegrams. And I believe that it was an attempt that for whatever had already happened in those municipalities, that the presidents of those municipalities were to be blamed. And I think, to say the least, that it was unfair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get -- ever get any response to your reply to Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no reaction. And especially then -- and also with regard to an earlier event in June that I have not mentioned here but it had to do with a very difficult phone conversation I had with him. I mean, our relationship was very cold, so to say, and especially as of then we were just barely polite to one another. It would have been for the best if Mr. Karadzic had sacked me then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the nature of the phone conversation you had with Mr. Karadzic that was difficult?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over the past few days when we talked, I have always try to stick to the principle to answer the questions that were put to me, but I'm going to make an attempt and sum it up in a couple sentences. We mentioned the death of the late Drago Macar, who was the battalion commander of the Motorised Brigade of Gorazde, and for your information he was not killed in combat but a vehicle hit a mine, a reconnaissance vehicle hit a mine, and he was killed. And the soldiers from his own battalion, I don't know how many people there were there, was kind of reluctant to go on after his death, which is kind of logical, and they decided to go back to Sokolac. So it was at some point on the 5th or 6th of June Mr. Karadzic phone and I picked up the phone, and I did not know what was going on at the time. And he said to necessity in an angry voice that I should immediately implement all measures in order to stop the forces withdrawing or coming back from Gorazde, otherwise I would be shot. I was really shocked by that sort of conversation, especially as I didn't know what was going on. And my answer was: Mr. President, you do what you like -- you can do whatever you like, but I have no way of doing what you're asking me to do. I was not the one who sent the armed forces to Gorazde. I'm not in command of those armed forces, and, quite simply, I don't know what's going on. He repeated his threat several times. I stuck to my original position and he rang off afterwards. Obviously I didn't do a thing, and quite soon I found out that the soldiers had already come almost to Sokolac, five or six kilometres away. On that day, for the first time, I seriously thought about resigning my job, but keeping in mind the fact that war was raging everywhere and that there were all sorts of problems and issues everywhere, and the assembly, the Municipal Assembly was not working. I knew that by doing that I would contribute an even greater degree of chaos and disorder. And therefore I decided to hang in there and continue in the job that I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, let me turn next to the village of Novoseoci. Was that the last Muslim village against which the operations of the 2nd Romanija Brigade were conducted?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Novoseoci.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not directing the witness's attention to any part of that packet, by the way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing, Mr. Prosecutor, since the Muslims remained in the bordering village, Vrh Barje, up until the end of 1994 almost, and it is the last village in which crime was committed in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, just for clarification, it seems the usher is directing the witness's attention to a document at the moment; that was not my intention. I was just going to ask the witness some questions about Novoseoci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So there's no need to consult any document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, do you recall whether that was early or late September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us what you know about what happened in Novo -- sorry, we didn't get an interpretation, although --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We're having some technical difficulties I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I did not receive any information -- not any interpretation. And on channel 4, I do not hear my own voice, which is not bad but ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said that this happened on the 22nd of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The answer has now been translated. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, can you tell us what happened at Novoseoci on September 22nd, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about the crime in Novoseoci in the evening hours of that same day from one soldier from the Romanija Brigade that was in that sector and they were preparing fuel, wood, for their families. As they were returning by that area, they passed by the crime scene and they saw the bodies scattered around. They probably recognised some of those bodies, and that's how they knew that the bodies belonged to the people of Novoseoci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over the course of the next couple of days, did you learn from other soldiers or any other source that you can tell us about what had happened at Novoseoci?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that day until this very day, in Sokolac and in Republika Srpska, the incident in Novoseoci is a taboo subject. However, we learned on the grapevine that the night before, members of the 2nd Romanija Brigade had blocked the village with some of their troops, and they carried out the operation on the 22nd of September. According to the information that I have, there was no armed resistance in the village. And then in the evening hours, after the women and the children had been transported by buses to Sarajevo, this unprecedented crime took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say the 2nd Romanija Brigade blocked the village the evening before, does that mean they essentially blocked access to it or surrounded it to prevent people from coming in or people from leaving?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. The village of Novoseoci is some eight or nine kilometres away from Sokolac. And from the Sokolac-Rogatica road, it is some four or five kilometres away. The village is somewhat separated from all the other villages, and it was no problem to surround it completely, in full secrecy even.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you indicated that the women and children were apparently separated from the men in the village and the women and children transported by buses to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men were the victims of what you described at the end of your earlier answer as "this unprecedented crime"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number; however, the figure that is mentioned is 45. I don't know whether that figure is correct or not. The media in the Federation followed the event, and especially when there was the exhumation of these bodies provided different figures. But I believe there is some 40 or so victims altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you learn whether the men were killed in the village or murdered elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The crime scene is some five or six kilometres away from the village. It is next to the Sokolac-Rogatica road in the Ivan Polje sector, not far from the road, maybe a couple hundred metres away from it as I was told. The crime scene is the landfill site that had existed there since 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Landfill, you mean that's a garbage dump?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a garbage dump. This is where all the garbage from the town was being taken by the utilities company. Earlier Sokolac and Rogatica had a common garbage site. However, in 1990 and in 1991 the situation was very difficult. And for economic reasons and for the lack of fuel they could not transport the garbage that far, and this location was opened as a temporary measure. During the month of May at the meetings of the Crisis Staff, we discussed this issue because the vicinity of that garbage site close to the road --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, the question was whether it was a garbage dump. You started your answer says: "Yes, it's a garbage dump." Then you told us a lot about the history of joint garbage dumps, et cetera, which is not of great assistance to the Chamber. If any further detail would be needed, then Mr. Tieger will certainly ask you for it. We are under some time restraint; I hope you will have understanding for that. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Novoseoci have a mosque before September 22nd, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a -- the most recently built mosque in the area of Sokolac. It was completed a few years before that and the villages started using it as of then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to that mosque?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mosque was blown up. I don't know whether the construction material remained in the place or whether it was removed. I believe that it was removed like from so many other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Blown up by members of the 2nd Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The engineers of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many mosques had there been in Sokolac municipality at the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were five mosques.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by the time the mosque at Novoseoci was destroyed by the 2nd Romanija Brigade, how many mosques remained in Sokolac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None. I believe that during these operations that we have just discussed, the others had already been destroyed. I am not sure about the one in Kosutica village, which is close to the Sokolac-Han Pijesak road. I don't know whether this was blown up before the one in Novoseoci or afterwards. In any case, within the scope of a few days there were no mosques in the territory of Sokolac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, can you tell the Court, give the Court any insight into why these mosques were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a belief among the Serbs that if there are no mosques, there are no Muslims. And by destroying the mosques, the Muslims will lose a motive to return to their villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to the next exhibit in a moment, but before I do I want to ask you who the commander of the 2nd Romanija Brigade was in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the 2nd Romanija Brigade was Mr. Krstic. I don't know whether his rank was colonel or lieutenant-colonel. I believe that he was a lieutenant-colonel at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know his first name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radislav Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next document would be ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like to turn to tab 6, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tab 6, that would get number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be exhibit P844, with the translation P844.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Tupajic, have you found tab 6? You may have noticed that the B/C/S version is at the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, tab 6 contains a B/C/S document and an English translation of a document signed by you and dated October 9th, 1992. Can you tell us, please, what that document is? And I'm referring to P844.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reference is made to my resignation to the position of the president of the municipality. I sent this document to the Municipal Board of the Serbian Democratic Party of Sokolac and the war commission of the municipality of Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you send this document, Mr. Tupajic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that I had seriously considered my resignation already in June 1992. However, after all this had happened in the village of Novoseoci, and bearing in mind all the other developments, I simply no longer felt capable of performing my duties any further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the third sentence of that letter you stated that: "I am no longer willing to accept the fact that so many harmful events have been going on at the territory of the municipality and that I cannot change the course of events."

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you referring to the events that you've described to the Court during the course of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so, Mr. Prosecutor. I primarily had in mind what happened in the village of Novoseoci and a number of other situations that I mentioned in my earlier interviews I may not have mentioned on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the second paragraph of that letter, there's a sentence that begins: "Since I have realised that the basic strategies and syntagm are not adjusted to present times." And you go on to say you think the post should be given to someone else who can bear the heavy burden. What did you mean when you said that the basic strategies are not adjusted to present times?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about my personal views as a human being, believing that they were not in line with what was going on in Sokolac and in Bosnia-Herzegovina. What I had in mind was that I could no longer bear all those things, that I could not come to terms with those things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the members of the Municipal Board respond to your submission of this letter?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no official reaction at all. My letter was obstructed. However, in my -- in verbal contacts I was told that there was no reason for me to do that and that bearing in mind the difficult moments that we were facing at the time I should not do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you told verbally by the members of the Municipal Board that you shouldn't do that because you were such an effective local leader or because that your resignation at that time and this letter would have some other kind of detrimental effect?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both parts of the reason are probably true. My resignation would have opened a number of other issues, which were then secret and some of which are still secret. Likewise, they could not have any objections to my part of the job, the job that -- the job that I was in charge of. I really did my utmost to put in place the conditions for people to be fed and the risk that was necessary in the face of very adverse conditions that prevailed at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your resignation letter seen by members of the Municipal Board, with whom you talked, as a condemnation of the policies that then existed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was the position. I suppose that there had been consultations with the superior officials, and they were very determined. I had insisted for a long time on all that, but they were determined when they asked me to withdraw my resignation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you eventually withdraw your resignation, and if so, why?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. In the meantime, there was another incident that I personally found very grave. My car was blown up one evening. I don't know whether this was done on purpose in order to kill me or just to warn me very seriously that I should stop insisting on my resignation. I don't know what the intention was. After that, I was more concerned of the well-being of my family than of my own well-being. I took this as the last warning, and I tacitly continued performing the duties that I had been performing up to then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tupajic, can you turn to tab 7, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can that be marked next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, P845, with the translation 845.1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, tab 845 -- or excuse me, P845 contains a report of an incident on November 12th, 1992, at 2205 hours in Sokolac. Does that reflect a report on the blowing up of your car, as you related to us?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. However, this was on the 12th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, and of course the document does reflect the 12th of October. Mr. Tupajic, did you report the massacre at Novoseoci to Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, or any other member of the Bosnian Serb or RS leadership?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not report to anybody about what had happened in Novoseoci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court why not, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For several reasons, perhaps. The first and the most important one was the fact that this happened towards the end of September 1992, and I personally and many others had information at the time that even uglier things and graver things had happened elsewhere in the municipalities that we have mentioned and in other municipalities all over Bosnia and Herzegovina. And that nothing had been done in order to punish the organisers and perpetrators of those crimes. The second reason was somewhat less important. It was my -- the reason of my own safety again. Earlier on on several occasions, I and my associates had been accused of having betrayed the military secrets of the 2nd Romanija Brigade, and I believe that a report of that nature would have been construed in the same way. This is the first time ever that any of the former or current officials of the Serbian Democratic Party or the Serbian republic is speaking about the crime that took place in Novoseoci. 16

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the first and most important reason why you didn't report the crime was the fact that this -- was the fact that even uglier and graver things had happened in other municipalities all over Bosnia and Herzegovina and that nothing had been done to punish the organisers and perpetrators of that -- of those crimes. In deciding whether or not to report the crime that happened at Novoseoci and the other crimes that happened in the municipality, did you consider whether or not Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and any of the other republican leaders had at least as much information about what had happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina as you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I believed that this was an obligation of the organs that we have mentioned, starting with the state security, the public security, and the military organs. I thought that they should use their lines of information to inform about various events, to inform their superiors and the most responsible people in various departments. And they in turn should have, and I believe that they did report about these events to the highest leadership of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I'm trying to be clear on this. When you told us that one of the reasons you didn't report it was that nothing had been done to punish the perpetrators of the grave crimes about which you knew in other municipalities, did that mean that you believed that the republican leadership knew about those crimes but didn't want to do anything to punish them --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that does rather lead on a flimsy foundation from the previous questions and answers, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, you told us that part of your basis for not reporting it was the fact that nothing had been done to punish the crimes about which you knew. Why then didn't you report it to Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, or any other republican leader so that something -- in an effort on your part to try to get something done about it, about Novoseoci?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't send any reports because I knew that nothing would be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. done in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I see that you're looking at the clock. How much time --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How much additional time would I need, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. Maybe 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just wondering whether we could perhaps finish before the break, then have the break a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have no objection to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and it's always encouraging if you know that there's a need for a break, to stick to the time limits. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I mention a very simple practical point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It may is seem trivial, but the canteen closes at 4.00, and if we are going to have breaks, it wouldn't be bad to have them when the facilities are available to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's -- well, if you're insisting on that, I'll do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not insisting, Your Honour. I'm just mentioning it. For everybody concerned, it is at least a small practical consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if you would promise me that you would be as strict after the break as you would be before without the special encouragement we would have a break, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no incentive needed to be as efficient as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, yes, we'll have a break until 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hope you enjoyed your afternoon tea.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I did. And I'm happy to say, Your Honour, the Trial Chamber was also represented in the canteen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I like to look after everybody --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I know how important afternoon tea for English people is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm delighted to see them as well, Your Honour. While we have a couple of minutes. Your Honour, may we make this request. Of course, Your Honour knows Mr. Josse's position in this case and he's been here. On the Defence side, it would be very helpful, and I would like very much Mr. Josse to deal with a witness who is coming up on Friday. I won't say the name because just all of a sudden I'm not 100 per cent confident whether it's open or closed. 537 is the number, Your Honour. Mr. Josse of course is not technically lead or co-counsel at the moment, but he is an English barrister of 20 years call. And would it be acceptable to Your Honour that Mr. Josse would deal with this witness for the Defence?.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will consider that. I would have -- personally now I'm speaking for myself, would have no problem. But I would like to inquire into any kind of registration as counsel would be needed at the registry, even if not assigned by the registry, I would try to find a solution such that there's a proper administration of the function of Mr. Josse in this courtroom because it might have some effect on other situations where in other cases someone comes with a good friend who is a good lawyer and who -- of course the Chamber is aware of the special situation here, but before we give a final decision on it, we would like to see that at least, in one way or the other, the position of Mr. Josse is formalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I very much appreciate that, Your Honour. Could I just say two things. First of all, I have myself spoken to the registry, who indicated at a pretty senior level, they have indicated to me that as far as they're concerned, if Your Honours are happy, there isn't a problem. I have also noticed sometimes in other cases that occasionally in special circumstances legal consultants in other cases have been permitted to address the court. But the first point, Your Honour, is -- well, it's no secret that it was Mr. Petrov I spoke to in the course of this afternoon, and of course he's on the Rule 45 list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Stewart, and then you'll hear from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do -- I do appreciate it very much. Is there a good chance that Your Honours would be able to let us know in the course of this afternoon? Because then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will at least discuss it during the next break, so I hope that -- it depends on whether we could reach an agreement during that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We're all in favour of agreement, but it's just the sooner everybody knows, the sooner they can get going on finalising preparation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. Then the witness may be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, we had just been talking about events in October of 1992 when you resigned and then when your car was blown up. I want to return very briefly to the summer of 1992 and ask you whether during that time the bodies of 37 Muslims were discovered in Sokolac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us quickly about that, how were they discovered and how were you informed, and what happened thereafter?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it happened in the month of May. I can't remember the exact date. But one morning Mr. Slobodan Batinic, who was the commander of the TO staff, and on the basis of that I can conclude it was in May because the TO staff was abolished on the 21st of May. Well, anyway, he came into my office at around 8.00 a.m. breathless basically and he said, Mr. President, do you know what had happened? And obviously I did not know, so I said, Tell me. I had no information. And From Ravna Romanija he was called and told that one of the farmers who took the animals, the cattle grazing, somewhere near Sabovski Grad came across dead bodies. And then he, Mr. Batinic I mean, did not tell me exactly who gave him that information. And I asked him, Well, do you know anything else about that? And obviously he said he did not. And we were both taken aback, shocked, by those news. And I said to him, Slobodan, please go and inform the police chief straight away and go and check the situation on the spot, and there's nothing else to do but make sure that the bodies are buried, and then, upon your return, report back to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how had these people been killed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we don't know the details, but on the basis of what he saw and what he told me, we assumed -- I mean, those were civilians; they were wearing civilian clothes. And we supposed they must have been taken there by some kind of vehicle and they were by the roadside. And we knew that they were from some other territory because Mr. Batinic did not recognise a single person. And because of his duties, because of the job that he had for about 20 years at the TO staff and as a commander for a very long time, he knew almost every single person in the municipality of Sokolac because of their military service and all that. And he said to me, President, these people are not from our area. And then he mentioned a figure, about 30 or 35 people. I don't think he actually counted them one by one. And on the basis of some other information we got later on and through the media from Sarajevo, and especially when exhumations started taking place in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and especially in the course of the stay of Mr. Miller as the US ambassador in the BH when there was fairly in-depth investigation on the group of Bosniaks who had disappeared; they had been taken somewhere from the part of Sarajevo called Nedzarici. So on the basis of all that, my conclusion was that it was possible that those people who were killed at Ravna Romanija on that occasion could have been that group from Nedzarici. About two years ago a newspaper from Sarajevo, Slobodna Bosna, wrote an article about that event. I don't know what their source of information was, because this event too is something that I'm talking about publicly for the first time. It has never been talked about in the Republika Srpska so far. And fewer people know about it in Sokolac as well than about this other event that we mentioned earlier in Novoseoci. Two years ago, since I provided that information at that stage as well when I was passing through that road in the direction of Sarajevo. And on one day I noticed a couple of European police vehicles which were precisely at the point of juncture between that macadam road and the highway. As to whether they were doing anything in terms of exhumating [as interpreted] bodies or whatever, I'm not aware of that. The only thing I was concerned about at that stage was that, for example, when I come back from The Hague I might run into even greater difficulties. And I was having quite a few difficulties when I first came back from The Hague to begin with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, just very quick follow-up or clarifying questions. First of all, what ethnicity were those people?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Second, you said they were killed. By what means were they killed? Were they shot or something else?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of what Mr. Batinic reported back to me, they were shot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, what was done with the bodies in 1992 after their discovery?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bodies were buried on the spot where they had originally been found. I believe, and that is what Batinic told me, I think that they used some road-digging equipment from the Romanija Putevi company, and I think that they buried the bodies there on the spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to return now, as we were discussing before, to the autumn of 1992. You mentioned in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tieger, I do apologise. Were those people only men? We haven't heard about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, I believe you heard the Judge's question.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is only men, on the basis of what I was told, or rather, what Mr. Batinic told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during your earlier testimony you mentioned meetings and visits by Mr. Krajisnik during 1992. Can I ask you to turn next to tab 8 of the materials in front of you. And, Mr. Tupajic, I would direct your attention to the two pages that are marked 0115-1435 and 1436. And you'll find those markings both toward the top of the page. And in the English translation it would be pages 8 and 9 of that series. Page 8 begins with a notation "12 November 1992," and page 9 begins with the words "solution for."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And those are the pages I would like marked as the next exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the original document number 0115-1435 and 0115-1436 will be given Prosecution Exhibit P846 and the translation on page 8 and 9 will be given 846.1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, was it your intention just to tender these pages or the whole package?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just those pages, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just those pages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, you see the two pages I was referring to, 0115-1435 and 0115-1436. The first page has a notation at the top of November 11, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, what I have here is the 12th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct. And as you'll see there's a stamped marking next to it which should say 0115-1435.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then we are on the same page. Can I ask you to turn to the next page, which is 0115-1436, and direct your attention to the second entry on that page next to an asterisk which says, Cyrillic letters: "In town urgent."

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what that entry reflects, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was a reminder for myself, after presumably a number of interventions on the part of Mr. Krajisnik, with regard to the fact that we should replace any indications or anything written in the Latin alphabet in the Cyrillic alphabet, and he probably said it urgently because it was a form of criticism that we had not done it before, because on a number of occasions beforehand Mr. Krajisnik always insisted that we should do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this particular notation made at the time or shortly after one of Mr. Krajisnik's visits to Sokolac and discussions with you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unable to claim that, but I do know that on the occasion of every visit he made to Sokolac, Mr. Krajisnik pointed it out to me and would make comments to that effect. My answer at that stage was, Mr. President - and I was half joking - we have more urgent matters to attend to, and we must allocate funds to more pressing matters at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any other visits to Sokolac by Mr. Krajisnik in the later part of 1992, that is November, December?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In December -- no, certainly there was a visit on the 19th of November and there was a religious holiday. And apart from Mr. Karadzic and General Mladic, Mr. Krajisnik was there as well. As to another visit with that two-month period, I can't recall at the moment. There was another visit earlier in conjunction with a misunderstanding that we once again had with the command of the Romanija Brigade. And Mr. Krajisnik came as a kind of peacekeeping or peacemaking mission. I can't remember exactly what time it was, what month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the five mosques in Sokolac municipality that had existed at the beginning of 1992 and that had been destroyed by September or the beginning of October 1992. When those mosques were standing, could any of them be seen from the main road?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the main road you could see two mosques: The one in Novoseoci, which is next to the road between Sokolac and Rogatica; and the other one in the village of Kosutica, which is next to the highway Sokolac-Han Pijesak-Zvornik. As to the others, they were close to local roads and they were impossible to see from the main road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you also mentioned in your earlier testimony that "Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik and other officials of Republika Srpska passed through Sokolac quite often on the road from Pale and Zvornik -- or from Pale to Belgrade." Is that main road -- is that the main road that we're talking about now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That road goes next to the village of Kosutica, where there was indeed a mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that Mr. Krajisnik was consistently insistent on changing Latin lettering to Cyrillic. Did Mr. Krajisnik ever mention to you anything about the mosques that had been destroyed and were no longer standing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever mention anything to you about the burned Muslim villages or the Muslims who were no longer in Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tupajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- that concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, when I just get myself physically organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Stewart, counsel for the Defence. Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, you at the very beginning of your evidence this week, you ran through some main dates in your political career. You'd been elected to the National Assembly in 1996 and been president of the SDS Deputies' Club from 1998 until last year. You became a member of the SDS Main Board in 2002. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's the first time that you had membership of that -- of that board?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you removed from your positions, your political positions, by the high representative?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened on the 29th of June, last year. I was hospitalised at Kasindol, as I had a heart attack on the 18th of June, and so I was being treated there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your political career, as you've described it, what happened between 1993 and 1996? That's to say, what were your -- in a nutshell, what were your political activities during that period?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was the president of the municipality of Sokolac and was a member of the Municipal Board of the Serb Democratic Party at Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So clearly you remained a member of the SDS throughout the whole period?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm still a member of the SDS, but I cannot occupy any positions, nor do I indeed occupy any positions in the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From August 1990 when you first joined the SDS party until your political career was terminated by the high representative a year ago today, was there any break in your membership of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any concerns about the leadership of the SDS at any time from 1993 up to the 29th of June, last year?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is not clear enough. What do you mean by "concerns"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll put a slightly different question. At any time from 1993 up to the 29th of June last year, did you have any concerns about the leadership of the SDS which led you to question whether you should continue as a member of the party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a person who is prone to self-criticism and also I'm always ready to address criticism to my friends, and that criticism is all with good intention. In certain situations, especially at the local level, I did always try to influence the work of the Municipal Board and the decisions that would benefit primarily the citizens of Sokolac municipality and Republika Srpska. I was more or less successful in doing that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have any particular power --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question, to put it in simply -- in simple words was: Did you ever think: I should resign as an SDS party member because of those leaders being at the top of it? That was the question, if I translated it --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I'm more than happy with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course there were situations in which I personally found myself in disagreement with some of the positions that were put forth by the leadership and the Main Board of the SDS. However, I always thought, and I still think, that it is better to be inside to try and act and change things, if at all possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you have seen yourself as some restraining or moderating influence on SDS policies, have you, during your -- the last few years of your political career?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my position as a deputy and the head of the club of deputies, I had the possibility to exert changes to the political agenda of the SDS. Through my work in the National Assembly, I believe I clearly demonstrated that because our work was very open to the general public, very transparent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was -- what was your personal -- what was your personal agenda? What did you personally hope to achieve in politics by becoming -- being elected to the National Assembly as an SDS member in 1996?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a very modest person. I don't have any political ambitions. I've never had any particular political ambitions. I believe that being a member of the National Assembly, which has been tested on several occasions on the open list was the confirmation of my very dedicated work in my previous positions. I've never had any ambition to rise to a high political position in any body of either Republika Srpska or Bosnia and Herzegovina. All these years I have lived during the war and after the war with the citizens I represented and I have led a quiet and modest life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you unambitiously became president of the SDS Deputies' Club, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you how this came about in a few sentences. This was in October 1998. We had a family tragedy at that time. My 18-year-old nephew died; he got killed. I believe that I got a call by Mr. Kalenic. I was in the village at the time. First he apologised for calling me at that moment, and he asked me whether I would be ready to assume the duties as the head of the SDS Deputies' Club. My answer to that was: If you and your associates deem that I can be successful in doing that, then I will certainly accept the position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, you were removed by the high representative, and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, we can produce copies of this over the next break as necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The actual decision of Lord Ashdown, the high representative, you were removed because in his view you were: "In whole or in part culpable for the SDS's failure to purge the political landscape of conditions -- of sustenance of individuals indicted under Article 19 as aforesaid and your failings were inimicable to stability and the rule of law. Milan Tupajic therefore obstructs the process of peace implementation and must be removed from office forthwith." Now, I take it that you are familiar with that element of the decision to remove you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the text of the decision. I have it with me here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you protest that as being unjust and unfair?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I appreciate that Mr. Ashdown is not completely satisfied with the political agenda or at least a part of it. I don't know which part of the political agenda of the SDS, although this political agenda has greatly changed lately with respect to the former times. I can say here that my contribution was very significant towards the vital reforms that have been carried out in Bosnia and Herzegovina lately. Let me mention but a few -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just before you -- before you do, Mr. Tupajic, you are in a particular category of relatively -- not very numerous category of people who have been removed indefinitely. 11 people have been -- were removed around that time indefinitely and can only resume a political career with the expressed sanction of Lord Ashdown or his successor. Correct?
