utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you have been active in trying to bring to justice individuals indicted for crimes during the conflict in former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I was going to talk about, and this can be easily checked with Mrs. Biljana Maric, I believe that that is her name; she is the Minister of Justice in the then-government of Mr. Mladen Ivanic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, can we first of all establish that your answer is -- do you say that your answer is, yes, that you have been active, leaving aside the details. Do you say, yes, you have been active in trying to bring to justice --

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you made representations --

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- in that respect to the high representative?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because neither I nor anyone else had an opportunity to do that, although there was a round table in Banja Luka, and I spoke to Mr. Ashdown and I told him what we did when the law on cooperation with The Hague Tribunal was being passed. And this is something I was going to tell you about when you interrupted me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, do you agree that since 1992 and 1993 you -- or in fact since the establishment of this Tribunal you have lived in some fear of being, yourself, indicted?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never lived in fear. I'm always ready to be held accountable for whatever I do. This is the kind of person I am; this is the way I behave. I was also aware of the fact that the time would come when the grave issues would be opened about the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that there would be an investigation, that there would be talks. And I knew, I was aware, that I would not be bypassed. As for whether an indictment would be issued or not, this was up to the investigators and those who were in charge of making such a decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, obviously, Mr. Tupajic. But my question -- let's downgrade it then. Do you agree that for a number of years you have lived under a degree of anxiety that you might well be among those indicted for crimes during the conflict in former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My answer is no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, that's unreal, isn't it? You know perfectly well that you are widely regarded as a potential -- as a potential criminal and somebody who could potentially be brought to justice for actions during that period, aren't you, and you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is your opinion. It may be shared by some others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you first come into contact with representatives of the Office of the Prosecution of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time it was in Banja Luka after a conversation with Mr. Trivun Jovicic who asked me whether I would be willing to talk to the investigators from The Hague. I said, of course, why not? And I asked him to let me know the time and the place, and that is what happened. That's what he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you said "why not," Mr. Tupajic because you knew perfectly well that it was a very dangerous thing for you to refuse, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I've just told you that given the position that I discharged at the time on behalf of the SDS, and I repeat, I knew that when the investigation started that the time would come for me to be given an opportunity to talk about what had happened in the territory of my municipality. I was absolutely aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were first interviewed by the Office of the Prosecution on the 2nd of December, 2002, you appreciated perfectly well, didn't you, that you were a suspect?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I was told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you regard yourself any longer as in danger of indictment by this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is up to the Tribunal. I believe that on the basis of the documents and everything they have at their disposal, they make a just and fair decisions. And I truly believe that in my case as well there will be justice and fairness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, isn't this the position, Mr. Tupajic, you personally as far as this Tribunal is concerned, you feel reasonably confident that you're in the clear and will not be indicted?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never discussed this issue with anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't feel the same confidence in relation to be being brought before a court in Bosnia and Herzegovina, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. This is not something that is on my mind at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the document which was put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it might be suitable if we were to put the -- Lord Ashdown's decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, does it add anything to what you've read? I have no problem to admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not insisting, Your Honour, at all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No disagreement, I take it, that the quotation is a correct one, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know that to be the case, but I have no reason to think otherwise. I am confident Mr. Stewart read it out correctly if he was reading from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I was, Your Honour. We printed it off the Internet. But we really -- it's from the official web site. We have no reason to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We leave it to you. But at least you have -- by putting these questions to the witness you have informed the Chamber about the reasons you learned for the dismissal of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- you were asked, Mr. Tupajic, about a document that's become commonly known as Variants A and B dated 19th of December, 1991. That had a previous exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness might have that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please assist Mr. Registrar, and we --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It came in from Mr. Tieger's list ... It's -- it was his item 1 on the list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's item 1, that's P43, P64A, P25 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 2529, B122, and also D10. So D10 might be the easiest to find.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have got the one, it was number 93, copy number 93, which was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have got one copy here. If it's put on the ELMO and if you please could assist the usher, Mr. Stewart, as to what page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. The -- I'm wanting to go to the third page at the moment, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, well, I'm so sorry. It's the third page of the English. It's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the witness it might be easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour is quite right. It's the third page of the B/C/S as well, including -- third page including the cover page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what you said -- first of all, Mr. Tupajic, you said -- this is page 10 of Tuesday's transcript. You said: "I'm familiar with the document, though I never had it on my files. It was sent by the Main Board to the presidents of the Municipal Boards. It was confidential." Now, first of all, do you in fact know that it was sent by the Main Board to the presidents of the Municipal Boards?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see in the document that the document was issued by the Main Board, and the body that issues such a document must send it, forward it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You see, Mr. Tupajic, I want to make it clear what my question is about. I'm not inviting you to tell us at this point what the document says or what you infer from what it's -- how it's labelled. I'm asking you -- or I'm putting it to you that you don't know who sent it to whom, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the technicalities of the way this document was sent. However, if it was adopted by the Main Board of the SDS, then there was a professional service sent the text of this instruction. I don't know how they did it, whether they did it by recommended letters or by hand or some other way. But it was sent to the presidents of the Municipal Boards. I apologise, Mr. President, I was interrupted earlier on when I wanted to say a few things that were very important and that I as the president of the club did in the Assembly. One sentence was taken out of the context. There is a lot more that went into my removal, and I believe that these things need to be explained so much from me, and I apologise for this --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't mean to stifle the witness unfairly. I'm in Your Honour's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll do that at the end. If there's anything to be added in relation to your removal, you will have an opportunity to tell us at the end. But Mr. Stewart is now allowed to continue. At the same time, Mr. Stewart, it seems that the witness has not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... how the document was -- how it travelled from its origin to its destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's -- I can leave that point then, if we can proceed then on that footing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- you say: "I believe that we discussed this document at the sessions of the Municipal Board, but we, members of the Municipal Board, were never familiarised with the integral text of the instruction." Mr. Tupajic, are you saying that the Municipal Board never sat down with this document in front of it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had it, and on the basis of that I conclude that no other members of the Municipal Board had the text of the document before them. It is a fairly common practice for some documents to be discussed at the sessions of the Municipal Board or other sessions, if those documents are confidential, to be kept by the chairman, because if such documents were to be distributed in 30 copies it was quite possible that they would no longer be confidential after that. And I believe that this was the case with this document as well, that the president kept it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's stick with knowledge as far as possible, Mr. Tupajic, if that's different from belief here. Who was in the chair at meetings or sessions of the Municipal Board between the end of December 1991 and the beginning of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, the first president of the Municipal Board which was elected at the Assembly was Mr. Mirko Malovic. He chaired the sessions while he was there. At the beginning of 1992 he went to America, and from then on the chairperson was Milovan Bjelovac [sic] until the moment he was removed, sometime in March of 2003.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what point. You say at the beginning of 1992. As accurate as you can, when did Mr. Mirko Malovic leave to go to the United States?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know the exact date of his departure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, there seems to be a problem as far as the year is concerned. March was translated as March 2003. It now disappeared from the transcript. Page 52, line 8. When did you say that the successor chairperson was removed? Was that in March of what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milovan Bjelica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- was removed from all the positions by the high commissioner as far as I know in March of 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So he held that position for some 11 years. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to press you a bit, Mr. Tupajic. This was -- in the local politics of Sokolac, it was quite a significant event, wasn't it, that the president of your SDS Municipal Board left to go to the United States?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't attribute any special importance to that. Mr. Mirko Malovic very fairly at the electoral Assembly, and I remember that very clearly, informed all the members of the Assembly that was electing him as president that some time ago he had submitted a request for the departure to America and that he was expecting in the coming months that his request would be approved and that he might well leave. And apart from that he was elected by the Assembly as president, and Mr. Milovan Bjelica was the deputy president. When Mr. Mirko Malovic left, Mr. Milovan Bjelica took over, and for 11 years now he's been leading the Municipal Board of the SDS in Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this period of rather unusual events, can you even put a month on Mr. Malovic's leaving his position as president of the SDS Municipal Board?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I couldn't remember exactly, but in the first few months of 1992, I can't remember whether it was January or February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you say then that either or both of those gentlemen then, as -- in the chair as the president of the Municipal Board, had in front of him at some point this Variants A and B document while it was being discussed by you and your colleagues on that board?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In January, February, and March, or at some time during that period. Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had it then and presumably it was in the archives of the Municipal Board. I don't know. I don't know what happened to it later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you, Mr. Tupajic, and none of your other colleagues asked to actually see this document during that period when it was under discussion? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We as members of the Municipal Board were basically acquainted with the substance of what was in that document and we knew what we were supposed to know. I can't remember all the details about that because after all it was as long as 13 years ago, maybe even longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, this is complete fabrication. You did not sit down as a body and discuss this document or any form of this document during that period, December to April 1992, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I do apologise. I'm not fabricating anything here. I did say these past few days that we carried out certain activities, following the instructions that are included in that document. I mean, I did not quite say that. What I did say was that I never had in my possession this form of document. And I think that this is understandable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, your -- do you agree your reason for security and not disseminating copies of this document, if it were to be passed around the table for you all to look at and handed back to the chairman, that would have retained security, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your point, but if a document is copied we have about 30 members of the Municipal Board, if you make 30 copies and you circulate it to the members of the Municipal Board and then they go away and take it out, it is no longer a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it handed back at the end of the meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have misunderstood Mr. Stewart. Mr. Stewart says there's no logic in the reason you've given because if that one document which was in the hand of the chairperson would have circulated without having been copied around the table, then you would have seen it and there would have been no additional security risk. That's what he puts to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I agree that it could have been done. I don't know whether it was done in that way or whether it was just the summary or the document in its entirety that had been read out by the president. The only thing I said was that I never had it in my files, and that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the Chamber is of the opinion that this matter has been sufficiently dealt with. Would you please move to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With great respect, Your Honour, I completely agree and I was just moving on to the next point, but still on this document, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, it was put to you that a number of steps that were taken in Sokolac were in pursuance of this document or an implementation of this document. I'm going to put it to you generally, in the interests of pressing on, Mr. Tupajic, not a single step that you described in your evidence was taken specifically in pursuance of this document; it just happens that some of the things that were done do coincide with some of the instructions in this document. That's the truth of the matter, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me just put this to you then, Mr. Tupajic, do you agree that if it had been intended by the Municipal Board to actually implement this document, it would have been just obvious, practical common sense, to go through it item by item and check them off, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it could not have been done in that way because certain activities are referred to there that were supposed to be carried out over a number of months and not within another period. I'm not sure I quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, you have now since whenever, you have studied this document at some point, have you, gone through it, seen what's contained in it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, but I didn't actually go into every detail because there is a great deal of repetition as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about the arrangements, and this was in reference to Exhibit 828, but you talked about -- I'm going to go into it for a moment, you talked about the arrangements made for members of the Sokolac Crisis Staff in relation to military service. And you said that, this is page 14 of Tuesday's transcript, yesterday's transcript, you said that: "All able-bodied men fit for military service had to be registered and had to have a certain assignment. We," and then going on a few lines to the foot of that page. "We received information from Mr. Ceranic, head of the Crisis Staff, that in view of the work we were doing we will have the benefit of service time spent in this job being counted double as other mobilised people have. I asked on that occasion that we receive more detailed information on what we were supposed to do from the body that set up the Crisis Staff in the first place." And what was that body that set up the Crisis Staff in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was set up on the basis of an order that came from Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you saying that when you -- you asked -- this is your evidence after all. You asked to receive more detailed information from the body that set up the Crisis Staff in the first place. So do you mean that you asked that you receive more detailed information from Dr. Karadzic? Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I said that I must have implied that. Because the order to set up Crisis Staffs in all municipalities originally came from him, and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was more detailed information obtained from Dr. Karadzic about the way in which your service time on the Crisis Staff might be counted for the purposes of your military service?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that we never asked for information from Mr. Karadzic in that respect. You are emphasising something that I just said in passing. Basically what we got from Mr. Ceranic was that all able-bodied men had to be assigned to some kind of duty. And he suggested that since we had already been set up following the orders from Mr. Karadzic, that we should be assigned to duties within the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Sokolac. And then he said, by the way, that there was a possibility which was not really of essential importance for us and it never came about because we never made an issue of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did this happen, this information that you got from Mr. Ceranic, head of the Crisis Staff, when do you say you got that information?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ceranic was a member of the Crisis Staff but he was the chief of the defence ministry department. It was at one of the meetings of the Crisis Staff. I don't have any documents in front of me; I just can't tell you off the cuff. I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The responses of the witness to which Mr. Stewart was earlier referring occurred after the presentation of the specific document, and I thought that might be of assistance if he's searching for a date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber yesterday wondered already to what extent bureaucratic procedures and double-counted time would greatly assist in determining this case. I was, as a matter of fact, referring to that yesterday when I was addressing the Prosecution. The Defence has put some questions on it now. Mr. Stewart, perhaps it's good for you to know that at least the subject of the bureaucratic accounting of years is not something that is at the top of the priority list of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's very close to the bottom of mine, and I thought it would have been apparent that it's not the bureaucratic procedures which are the points of these questions. They are simply the underlying background and context that this was about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not interested, Your Honour, on the Defence's part at all in these bureaucratic procedures for themselves --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- the Chamber would highly appreciate if that could become perfectly clear from questions and hopefully from answers as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm in favour of the latter as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When do you say that Mr. Ceranic -- Mr. Ceranic was at some point head of the Crisis Staff, was he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was the president of the Crisis Staff throughout. Mr. Ceranic, according to his position as head of defence ministry department, was also the head of the Crisis Staff throughout.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, correction, a member, not the head. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction which I was -- I was really struggling there before that correction, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tupajic, relief all around I think. The -- page 14, line 25, you don't have that in front of you. Yesterday when you said: "We received information from Mr. Ceranic, head of the Crisis Staff," that's a slip or an error somewhere and he never was, he was a member, you were the head. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described -- again, it relates to a document P832 concerning the Sokolac psychiatric hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I make it clear, I'm not the least bit interested in the details of organisation of the hospital or treatment of patients or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said it was the ministry -- this is page 21 of yesterday's transcript, line 3: "It was the Ministry of Health and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina who were supposed to deal with the problem but we ourselves took it upon ourselves to collect information and to forward this information to the competent ministry and the government that would then try and solve at least part of the hospital's problems." And the ministry was very obviously the Ministry of Health, wasn't it, Mr. Tupajic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Plus the initiative to try to and solve the problem of how many people, and they were crowded at the hospital, came from the hospital director.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the minister was Mr. Kalenic at the time, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And none of these issues relating to this hospital, financial, or other organisational issues in any way involved Dr. Karadzic or Mr. Krajisnik, did they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the organisation and the duties within the framework of the work of the government, no. But the government was accountable to the National Assembly for their work, and of course the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Tupajic, that does sufficiently answer my question. And we see in that document, that's P832, I won't trouble unless somebody else wants me to put it in front of you. Item 2 there says: "Authorised employees of the psychiatric hospital are to take care of all the patients until a solution to financing the hospital and its further status has been found." All the patients, apart from anything else, was -- to make clear, wasn't it, Mr. Tupajic, you've signed this document, to make clear that that was without discrimination on any grounds of ethnicity or nationality, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the person who had the most -- this is at page 29 of yesterday's transcript and you were being asked by Mr. Tieger, you said that you'd looked at -- the question of reports to the republic level and interaction with the republic level. And then you said that the person who had the most contacts with the SDS leadership and the leadership of Republika Srpska was Milovan Bjelovac and then Mr. Marko Simic who was a deputy and the first president of the municipality of Sokolac. So you're putting it in that order, are you, that Mr. Bjelovac [sic] had the most contact and then second to him in degree or extent of contact was Mr. Simic? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but maybe I should make a correction. It was Mr. Milovan Bjelica, not Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. It's a mistake in the transcript, Bjelica, the same gentleman we've been talking about. You're nodding. That appears to be confirmed. Then you said: "Members of the Crisis Staff had occasional contacts but mostly with the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." When you're talking there mostly with the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you were talking, were you, of contacts with ministries over specific issues, such as the hospital issue that we were considering a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, amongst other things. The hospital issue and a whole range of other issues as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the sort of issues, do you agree, that though they may have been affected by the particular difficulties of the situation in early 1992 the sort of issues which arise in peacetime as in wartime?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Basically we had a war situation throughout, and any attempt to implement peacetime laws, regulations, and relationships always caused us quite a few difficulties on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have personal knowledge of the contacts that were made by Mr. Bjelica with the SDS leadership and the leadership of Republika Srpska in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I've mentioned this before. I can't claim that it happened on a daily basis, but Bjelica had frequent contacts with the leadership of the Serb Democratic Party, especially with Mr. Karadzic. We also had the opportunity to witness one of those conversations. And later on, in later years, he had a job at Pale and he went to Pale every day and he spent time there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can you say from your own personal knowledge about contacts between Mr. Bjelica and Mr. Krajisnik in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only refer to meetings that we attended together. I know that they did have other contacts, presumably less often than with Mr. Karadzic, but they certainly had contacts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us what the basis of your knowledge is. Leave aside the meetings of which you give evidence yourself, what can you -- what's the basis of your own knowledge then that they certainly had other contacts?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know -- I mean, of course you will ask me to refer to specific occasions, but the atmosphere and the overall situation was such as to require these contacts, and therefore those contacts happened. As to the details of all that, I can't really talk about it and especially when it comes to meetings and the details of meetings that I myself did not attend. But I know on the basis of my conversations with him, I know that he was entertaining a normal sort of communication with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, perhaps we could clarify this issue and then have a break. It's 20 minutes to 6.00. Mr. Stewart asked you how did you know about all these meetings. He didn't ask for any details as far as the content is concerned. He just wanted to know those meetings where you were not personally present, how did you know about the other meetings Mr. Bjelica had with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, but I -- the question is clearly a response in direct -- directly addressed to that question in the latter part of the witness's answer. I don't know if the Court is directing the witness's attention to something else, but it seems to me the last sentence is a direct response to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps I may have overlooked it because I was preparing for my intervention. I might have not sufficiently, carefully listened to the witness. When you said that: "But I know on the basis of my conversations with him," did you refer to conversations with Mr. Bjelica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And he told you that he had these meetings with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, don't -- I'm not sure the word "meetings" came into it. I say I'm not sure. I'm being careful --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I do agree. He said "entertaining a normal sort of communication with him." But he said that in the context of questions about meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not quite. I had mentioned meetings in order to exclude them. He had mentioned the meetings and I said "leaving aside the meetings."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you say that he told you that he was entertaining a normal sort of communication with Mr. Krajisnik, what kind of normal sort of communication he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Your Honour, yesterday we had an intercept here. And in the course of that intercept there is a reference between -- to contact, to communication between Mr. Bjelica and Mr. Krajisnik; that was in just one intercept. So when I'm saying, for example, that when it came to oil supplies or whatever, because Mr. Bjelica unofficially for a long time was managing the Romanija petrol company that was in charge of supplying fuel to the municipality. And so he always talked about these matters to Mr. Krajisnik or to his brother, and there must have been a whole host of other issues like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What there must have been is a different matter. He told you that he had communication with Mr. Krajisnik; it could be any kind. It could be telephone conversations, it could be writing letters to each other, it could be personal meetings. Did he tell you what these communications were? Were those meetings? Were those telephone conversations? Were those correspondence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Less about correspondence. I can't recall all the details, but at that time it was normal. We talked about it and I do know that they were in touch. I can't say what exactly they talked about and how many times, but I do know that they were in touch --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that for certain and probably quite often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The issue is how they were in touch. Did he say, We meet? Did he say, We call each other by telephone? Or don't you remember? Then it's ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he did not have a duty to tell me anything, nor was he reporting to me on anything whatsoever. I concluded that on the basis of what we talked about. And I think he often met with Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps more often with Mr. Karadzic at Pale because he was one of their -- of the people they trusted, and especially that Mr. Karadzic trusted, and everybody knows that, and presumably there were quite a few meetings that I never knew of, and that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I now do understand your testimony that you concluded from your conversations with Mr. Bjelica, although it is not clear to you anymore on what details you came to such a conclusion, that the contacts he had with Mr. Krajisnik would include meetings, although not as frequent as meetings with Mr. Karadzic? Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a break until five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you asked whether you could receive an answer to your request. I think you get it within the next two or three minutes, because it's not without hesitation that the Chamber dealt with the matter. First of all, and I'm addressing you and perhaps Mr. Krajisnik as well, of course the Chamber is aware that conversations were held in order to try to find a solution for some of the matters that were bothering Mr. Krajisnik, and one of them was the constitution of the Defence team. We have not been recently informed about any further progress, although at the time we understood that quite some progress was made and that the solution was almost there. Before the Chamber enters into any such, I would say, exceptional situation where someone who is not either registered as chosen counsel or assigned as counsel by the registry, before we enter into that, we at least would like to know whether an agreement is nearby or not, because otherwise it would not be a good idea to start these kind of experiments. That's the first question. So I'm addressing you and Mr. Krajisnik whether we could expect a kind of solution soon as far as the registry is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I -- I can't answer that, Your Honour. The -- Mr. Krajisnik, I know is having discussions -- we met this morning. I know he's got further discussions. I can't really answer that, Your Honour. Of course progress has been made. Certainly as far as my discussions with the registry are concerned, considerable progress has been made, but they're all interrelated, Your Honour, so I can't say that. But what I can say, Your Honour, perhaps I should have mentioned that, that Mr. Krajisnik of course can speak for himself, although of course it remains my position that it's primarily my job to speak for him. Your Honours know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I know that. But at the same time when he's involved in these type of discussions --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was simply going to say that it has been discussed. We've been up together to the UNDU. Mr. Krajisnik has indicated that he is entirely happy for Mr. Josse to do this witness on Friday. He can certainly confirm that himself, but I can report that to Your Honour in relation to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I -- we never expect counsel to say anything else, but if you'd like to add something to what has already been said, then please do so but let's not spend too much time on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did have a meeting with the representative of the registry. This meeting was successful. We're supposed to continue tomorrow, and we -- I believe that we will deal with all the issues that are still pending. One of the issues was Mr. Josse, and what Mr. Stewart has just said is correct. I hope that I will see a positive outcome and that's why I said that I would be glad if Mr. Josse could examine the witness. I would like to commend the representative of the registry, who has been very flexible in seeking solutions, and that's why we have been able to deal with a number of issues so fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. Then finally, the Chamber is inclined, given these circumstances, to allow Mr. Josse to act as counsel. He is qualified as a -- he is a member of the bar of England, I think it's the bar of England and Wales, if I'm well-informed. So therefore he can act. It's with the consent of Mr. Krajisnik. The messages we received from the registry is that they do not oppose, because usually if a counsel not assigned would act, of course that might -- might not be in a normal situation where assigned counsel are defending and not at the same time chosen counsel. So that seems not to be a problem as far as the registry is concerned. Then a final issue which is of importance for the Chamber is that if it were only for two or three days we would like to have Mr. Josse on the list as a member of the Defence team at this moment because this creates obligations in terms of confidentiality. You are, as a starting point, although Mr. Josse has been here, we also know that at an earlier occasion when matters were less clear when we were in closed session, which we prefer not to have anyone there. So even if it would be on a temporary, provisional basis, we would like to have Mr. Josse on the list of members of the Defence team, which means that he has access to whatever confidential material and that he is also bound by --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, he already is

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He already is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He already is and has been for some considerable time, Your Honour. I'm sorry, perhaps I should have made that clear. There's absolutely no problem about that. And of course Mr. Josse's membership of the Defence team is then of course bolstered up by his obligations as a member of the English bar -- English and Welsh bar in relation to such matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both. It qualifies him to act before this Tribunal and at the same time it adds to the professional duties he has to fulfil.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I just add one other matter, Your Honour, and Mr. Josse wants to add a matter, and it's a different one, through me; I appreciate that. The -- which is that he won't be -- although he would be more than capable of doing it, he won't be on his own, Your Honour. He'll be accompanied -- it looks as if it's going to be Ms. Loukas who will metaphorically hold his hand on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. And I took the whole of this exercise --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps I mentioned earlier, Mr. Josse is already on the Rule 45 list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's no problem. The messages we received from the registry is that there are no concerns in this respect. I took it because this is -- well, I will say taking some steps already in advance of matters we expected to be formalised as soon as possible. I take it that this is discussed with the whole of the Defence team and that there's no disagreement on Mr. Josse next Friday, because here many members of the Defence team are there but not all of them. And I take it that Ms. Loukas is aware and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, Ms. Loukas, certainly. Ms. Loukas wouldn't have been very delighted if the answer from the Trial Chamber had been different, Your Honour. But that's another matter. As far as the rest of the Defence team is concerned, Your Honour, it isn't a democracy, and the members of the Defence team Your Honour has mentioned have been consulted and are happy with the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wanted to -- you see that the Chamber had some hesitation and wants to proceed very cautiously in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We fully understand that and are very appreciative of the response, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we could ask Mr. Usher to escort the witness into the courtroom, and, Mr. Stewart, you may continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, Mr. Stewart will continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, you were also asked, and this is page 41 of the transcript yesterday. You were asked: "What did you understand Mr. Bjelica's relationship with Dr. Karadzic to be in 1991 and 1992?" And you said: "Well, this conversation," and that was the one about the petrol and so on, and we'll come back to that, "but this conversation, too, confirms that they had full, direct contact and they contacted each other on many issues." Mr. Tupajic, you don't really know, do you, whether or not Mr. Bjelica and Dr. Karadzic contacted each other on many issues?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not right, Mr. Stewart. I know that they had very frequent contacts and that Mr. Bjelica was amongst the people who enjoyed a lot of trust with Mr. Karadzic. And this was not the case only in 1991 and 1992; this continued throughout subsequent years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a particular history of their personal relationship which enabled Mr. Bjelica to have particularly close contact and dealings with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they had any relationship before the SDS was established. But it is a well-known fact in Republika Srpska that there is a relationship between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Bjelica. This is not something that I, myself, said; this is what all the prominent members of the SDS are fully aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica and Dr. Karadzic's contact on these issues then, did Mr. Bjelica discuss with you what those issues were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke and my impression was that only some of the conversations with Mr. Karadzic were related to me and only those that concerned the part of the job that I was supposed to do with my associates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what specifically was your part of the job then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you what the job of the president of the municipality. There are a lot of things to do, especially in the times of war. It will take some time, though, but if you insist, I don't mind telling you all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in that case, with the Court's permission, I won't insist then, Mr. Tupajic. I will ask you this: Please, sir, could you just give a couple of examples of issues that you know, leave aside the petrol thing, of issues that you know were discussed between Mr. Bjelica and Dr. Karadzic in 1991 and 1992. Just name two issues.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to personnel and appointment of people in the municipality, I believe that there are a lot of contacts about that, not only during the war but also in subsequent years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So personnel is one. What's another?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a wide range of issues that were discussed. I'm trying to remember --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I beg your pardon. I didn't mean to interrupt your train of thought. I just wanted one in answer to my question, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could tell that they talked about the behaviour of the local MUP in Sokolac. These conversations always concerned the analysis of the situation in Sokolac and measures that could possibly be taken with that regard. That's why I've said that there was a wide range of issues discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't know anything about this conversation between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Bjelica about the petrol, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only two days ago that I learned about this conversation, when I first heard that intercept and read the transcript here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't really know very much about what that's all about, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I shall repeat. Mr. Bjelica enjoyed a lot of trust with Mr. Karadzic, and I assume, which has been confirmed over the years, that this has remained the case. If somebody attends the most important Serbian religious holidays and celebrations, to which only the closest associates and relatives are invited, then this shows you what was the nature of a relationship between these two men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, that answer is really, with respect, nowhere near an answer to my question. I was putting it to you: You don't really know very much about what that conversation about Jugopetrol is about. You really don't know very much what that's all about, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about that conversation. However, when I heard it, things became absolutely clear. I believe there were other conversations about that same topic. I have mentioned that Mr. Bjelica had been involved in the traffic and sale of oil for a number of years, and that's why I believed that there were other conversations about that. I don't know how many. And I'm sure that there were other conversations between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Bjelica that I don't know anything about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- Mr. Tupajic, are you saying that anything you know about this Jugopetrol issue involves anything negative about Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know any details. I would not comment upon that. I have never been involved in any of that. However, I would like to illustrate this by saying as follows, if you insist. I remember what Mr. Bjelica told me after his first rest on the -- by the SFOR. He told me things that absolutely shocked me. It was the first time then that I learned that Mr. Radovan Karadzic had spent some time in Sokolac in 1998 and that Mr. Milovan Bjelica knew about that. He stayed in a building which is not more than 200 metres away from my building. I, myself, never knew anything about that. I'm sure that -- and there is a number of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. people who looked after him during his stay and who knew exactly what was going on. I'm giving you this just an illustration --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Tupajic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that doesn't seem to be remotely related to my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I do agree with you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is related. Of course it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the question was whether there's anything you know about this Jugopetrol that involves anything negative about Mr. Krajisnik. When you say that Mr. Karadzic may have spent some time in Sokolac, that's not really an answer to the question. So do you know in this respect anything, any negative thing, about Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, may I add just with respect to that I specifically said Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik to avoid any possible misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik who is here in the courtroom. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I've answered the question. I said that I don't know anything about that. In that conversation, the name is not mentioned, either of Mr. Momcilo or Mirko Krajisnik. I have never dealt with that issue. I apologise to the Chamber if I have provided information that is beyond the context. I was just going to give you an example of mistrust that was shown to me. And for that reason, I didn't know -- I was not aware of the contents and the gist of a number of conversations that took place between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Bjelica. And I apologise for having taking up too much of your time with this answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem, Mr. Tupajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, is it correct that you know more about contacts between Mr. Bjelica and people in Pale than you do about contacts between Mr. Simic and people in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Earlier in my testimony I said that Mr. Bjelica had more contacts with the leadership in Pale. The late Marko Simic, as a member of the Assembly probably had more contacts with Mr. Krajisnik, which is only logical. Later on he became a member of staff of the National Assembly and he had his tasks. And hence, my belief in my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just -- you were asked -- page 43 of yesterday's transcript: "Who were the candidates that oral information conveyed from the Republika Srpska leaders to Sokolac," and you said: "Oral communications came mainly through Mr. Bjelica and the late Mr. Marko Simic who was deputy to the National Assembly." Do you say that Mr. Marko Simic reported back to you on -- on matters involving the Republika Srpska leadership?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The late Simic did not have any duty to report to me. We would meet from time to time and inform each other on matters that were happening in the municipality and in the republic. There was no duty involved in any of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, in 1991 and 1992 have any direct contact with the Main Board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No contacts with the Main Board of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- you were asked -- this is page 51 of the transcript yesterday. You had an answer -- line 18 of that page: "When the army of Republika Srpska was established on the 12th of May, pursuant to this decision of the Assembly in Banja Luka and when Mr. Ratko Mladic was appointed head of the Main Staff, we were invited to this meeting, which was an official meeting," and you gave evidence about that, "a protocol meeting at which we met each other officially. We had very little time at our disposal, but the essence of the meeting was as was precisely that for us to meet." And then Mr. Tieger asked you: "Were other military officials there other than General Mladic?" And you said: "I can't remember, but I believe there was some of General Mladic's assistants there. He had just established his Main Staff. I can't be sure but I believe that Mr. Tolimir and Mr. Gvero were also there. I'm not sure. The establishing of the Main Staff was underway and many of the officers joined the Main Staff only after this meeting." Mr. Tupajic, is it correct that you have no significant knowledge yourself of the process of establishment of the Main Staff and who joined the Main Staff when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you what I know. Maybe I know more than I should, given the position that I held. The Main Staff was in the vicinity of Sokolac, and many members of the Main Staff would drop by occasionally. And the hospital of the Main Staff was also in Sokolac, and I would bump into them from time to time. What I know is that on the 12th of May the decision was issued to establish the Army of Republika Srpska. As for the details of the establishment of the Main Staff, the appointment of officers and its services, I don't know anything about that. Later on I was introduced to the majority of the Main Staff members, that was in the course of 1992 after its establishment and during the war years. In other words, I met with a majority of the members of the Main Staff on various occasions. I didn't meet with all of them but with a majority I did meet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever, yourself, receive any direction or order of any sort from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive an order, not only I but a few other municipal presidents, to organise the stacking of hay. That was in 1992 and 1993 in the general region of Suhareke and in the Vlasenic [phoen] area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said at page 31 of yesterday's transcript that you were asked: "Did the Sokolac SDS receive orders and directives and guidelines from the Main Board of the SDS in 1991 and early 1992?" And you said: "Yes." Do you say that you have personal knowledge of, in the first place, written orders or directives or guidelines received from the Main Board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a customary type of communication. Some documents adopted at the Main Board and for which it was considered that the Municipal Boards should be familiarised with were sent to the Municipal Board, either for their attention or for their elaboration. This was the practice then and it still exists; this is nothing new. I don't remember any specific details. The president of the party had that task, and he was in charge of the entire communication on behalf of the Municipal Board with the Main Board. Him and his associates from the professional services were involved in that, but this is nothing but a customary form of communication, which is only logical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you saying that the pattern of communication between the Main Board of the SDS and municipalities has been broadly the same throughout 1991, 1992, and the period ever since?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Your question is rather confusing. You said between the Main Board of the SDS and the municipalities. Are you referring to the Municipal Boards of the SDS or the municipalities as institutions in themselves?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tupajic. You're quite right. I should rephrase that question. Are you saying that the pattern of communication between the Main Board of the SDS and the Municipal Boards of the SDS has been broadly the same throughout 1991, 1992, and the period years ever since?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, that was the case. I don't think that there were any major differences in the way they communicated. There was no reason for them to change their way of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the morning we go to a quarter to, but in the evening we go until 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, so we do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it remains that I was looking at the clock, but then I'll carry on for another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The cafeteria is not open anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, there are other temptations, Your Honour, but I'll press on of course. Thank you for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- you were asked about -- this was at page 81 of yesterday's transcript, Mr. Tupajic. Mr. Tieger said to you: "At any point was a war commission," this is line 18, "formed in Sokolac?" And you said: "I don't understand your question, what commission?" And so on. And then Mr. Tieger said: "At any point in 1992 was anyone designated as a war commissioner sent to Sokolac?" And your answer was: "Yes, the so-called war commission was established. I don't remember when, and as far as I can remember war commissioners were members of the National Assembly. The war commission for Sokolac was Marko Simic." On the transcript it actually says the war commission for Sokolac was Marko Simic. "There were three others of us in the war commission. I believe that this was the way for them to get an insight into developments in the municipalities." Now, first of all, when you say "as far as I can remember war commissioners were members of the National Assembly," could you just explain that. Are you saying all war commissioners were -- I'll start again. When you say "war commissioners were members of the National Assembly," you're not talking there about Sokolac war commissioners, are you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that all MPs were commissioners and that it was an exclusive rule. But as far as I can recall, a certain number of MPs were indeed appointed as war commissioners, which in the last analysis is only logical since they came from the base, as it were, and they could be used as a stronger link between the base and the republican authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps we can take it in steps. When you talk about the war commission, you're talking about the body that effectively took over from the Crisis Staff, are you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. There seems to be a misunderstanding there. It was appointed at the time when the Crisis Staffs were in operation. I know of the situation in Sokolac whereby the Crisis Staff stopped working at some point mid-July. And before that time, the war commission had been set up and appointed. And basically, as far as I know, it did not do anything in particular, except perhaps analysing the work of the Crisis Staff and possibly informing the republican authorities and bodies. By the end of July, the executive committee or the Executive Board was set up and did continue to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take it in steps. Can you -- as best you can, when was a -- this was an SDS war commission. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the name for it was at the time, but it was appointed for the municipality of Sokolac and all the members were members of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was only Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As best you can, when was the Sokolac war commission established?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We looked at that document in the past few days here. I don't have it in front of me, so I can't tell you the exact date. I think at some point in June but I'm not certain. The Prosecution have that document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say there were four of you in the war commission, is that correct, four members?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remembered that when I saw the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was you, Mr. Simic, and who were the other two?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a Mr. Podinic, if I remember correctly, and Mr. Radomir Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Bjelica was not a member. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to the document we looked at, no, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it that not so much war commissioners were members of the National Assembly, which is what the transcript -- which is what your evidence was yesterday, but is it more accurate to say that deputies in the National Assembly were normally members of war commissions set up in their particular municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the situation in the other municipalities. I know that our own MP from Sokolac, the late Mr. Simic, was appointed as president of the commission. I don't know what the situation in other municipalities was. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday when you said - this is page 81, line 24 - what did you mean when you said: "As far as I can remember, war commissioners were members of the National Assembly." That's the entire sentence: "And as far as I can remember, war commissioners were members of the National Assembly." Please explain, what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant for Sokolac and perhaps a couple of other cases that I knew of where MPs were commissioners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all you're saying, leave aside for the moment these other couple of municipalities, all you're saying was that in Sokolac Mr. Simic, who was a deputy on the National Assembly, was the president, in fact, of the war commission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just to clarify when the answer to Mr. Tieger's question to you was: "At any point in 1992 was anyone designated as a war commissioner sent to Sokolac?" And you said: "Yes." There was no sense in which Mr. Simic was sent to Sokolac as a war commissioner, was there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was appointed by Mr. Karadzic, as far as I can remember, and that's what it says in the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was from Sokolac, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, who's arguing against that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nobody had to send him because that's where he started from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the Chamber is convinced that this extensive exploring the word "send" is in view of the evidence we have already heard is not of great assistance to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- you were asked, and this is at page 79 of the -- of yesterday's transcript: "What organs or bodies existed for the purpose of gathering information and communicating it to the top leadership of Republika Srpska?" And you said -- your answer was: "At the local level, meaning at the municipal level, there were state security departments which were organised into regional centres of state security, chiefs for regional security were responsible and reported to the chief of state security, who answered for his work and the work of his service to the president of the republic. The second line of information went from public security station via security services sent to the minister of the interior. Who he reported to, I don't know but I assume that he reported to the highest state organs. The third line of information was the military line of information starting with the lowest-level commands, via the brigade commands to the corps commands, and further on to the Main Staff, and therefrom, I suppose, a certain amount of information was forwarded to the state leadership." Mr. Tupajic, as far as those particular matters are concerned, do you agree that you have no special personal knowledge of what is in fact a description of just the structure of these organs and these bodies?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I've quite understood the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll put it another way then, preface it. Would you -- do you agree, what you have described there is the structure of various organs and various levels in Republika Srpska in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let me put it this way: Do you agree that really anybody who had any reasonably informed knowledge of the organisation of Republika Srpska could say exactly what you've set out in your evidence there? You have no special personal knowledge to add on these matters, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please. I'm somebody who was the president of the municipality, and as such I knew what institutions were set up and working in the Republika Srpska and how they operated, at least at lower levels. I'm not quite sure as to the top level, who was accountable to whom, who was meant to report to whom, in what way, and in what shape or form. But as to the existence of the security services centres and the police stations and all that and that the security services centres were accountable to the minister, it as something that is common knowledge to anyone who knows anything about politics. And this is the same way the police force is organised in the Republika Srpska even now, and up until a short time the security services and the military were organised in exactly the same way. I fail to understand what you're trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'm looking at the clock. We're close to 7.00. I would like to ask one or two questions not in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would this be a suitable time for you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course, no problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, we're not ready yet, as you may have noticed. We would like to see you back tomorrow in this same courtroom morning at 9.00. Mr. Usher, would you please escort Mr. Tupajic out of the courtroom but not until I -- could he please put the headphones on -- Mr. Usher, no, no no, no. Mr. Tupajic, I would like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given or you're still about to give tomorrow. That's what I wanted to tell you before you leave this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't worry, Your Honour. I'm fully aware of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, you may escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, could you give us an impression on how much time you would still need in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was just discussing with my colleagues and we -- that rather elastic phrase "not much longer," Your Honour. Your Honour, I'm confident that I will finish before the first break tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, how much time do you think you would need?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer, as usual, is I don't know. I'll do my best to keep it as brief as possible. I would just like to put a question to you if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I submitted some documents to both the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution. Would it be possible for those documents to be submitted to the witness as well in order to speed things up, unless it's out of order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, I have tried to look at them, although they are not translated. But, for example, I see one 19th of December document which has already been put to the witness, so there would be no need to do it again. I also noticed that apart from what seemed to be some -- some reports of the Assembly, the stenographic notes, I also see there is also quite a lot of publications, publications -- of course I haven't read them, but are not prohibited from presenting to a witness. But at the same time, this is not a case that will be determined on the basis of press reports but on what witnesses have to tell us. And sometimes confrontation with a specific press publication may be important, then it can be put to the witness. But I couldn't give you a general answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I raise a point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- unless Mr. Krajisnik tells me that there's something that I've overlooked, and he does occasionally tell me that, he says that these documents have been submitted to both the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution, but not so far, as far as I'm aware, to Mr. Krajisnik's counsel under the status quo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Usually the Chamber does not interfere between communications between counsel and accused, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that isn't the point. I'm reporting to the Trial Chamber the slightly and unusual circumstance that these documents have been submitted to the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I qualified what he was saying unless it hasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have overlooked something and it might be a similar matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll put it in the passive, something has been overlooked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: On this particular occasion I normally take the flak for everything, Your Honour, but here I speak in the passive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll put them on the list together with the maps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just explain, Your Honour. There seems to be a mistake because I did give it to the Defence team. They might not have seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik. When I said that I put this issue on the list together with the maps, that was the occasion where you were perfectly right that you had your own maps and there was no ground for what at that moment was said. So this is added to that list. Yes. I give you an answer to that. Finally, one question, is there any agreement between accused and counsel on how to split up the time for cross-examination? Because tomorrow Mr. Thompson is scheduled as a 92 bis witness as far as I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And if I could make one observation in response to Mr. Krajisnik's comment that he doesn't know how long he'll be but he intends to be brief, there do seem to be a great number of documents in here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can appreciate that Mr. Krajisnik may desire to use all or a large number of these documents, but he's in a position now to make the same judicious judgements about the use of time that everyone else here has to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I indicated before that I would appreciate if counsel and the accused would reach an agreement on the time they would use. I also remember at least some observations as to whether counsel would give any time away. I don't want that conversation to be repeated. The only thing that may be clear is that the Chamber allows some additional questions to Mr. Krajisnik. The Chamber has also indicated that this would not -- should not lead to more time spent on cross-examination than granted. And we know there's no 60 per cent rule, but there's 60 per cent guidance which we do not always follow, but we would like to go back to that. And the -- I don't know whether there would be any opportunity to see how you could do that, but if I look at the time spent in cross-examination -- in examination-in-chief, if I combine the information I've received about the time Mr. Stewart needs tomorrow and that Mr. Krajisnik would be brief, but brief is not always as brief as one would expect, then I'm afraid that we spent too much time on cross-examination. So you're invited to see whether you can reach any agreement. I know that communication might not be very easy. If you'd think that by waiting for another two minutes that would help so that you at least have an opportunity, where you might not be able to see each other once you've left this courtroom, I'll facilitate that. But as I also indicated, if this doesn't lead to any agreement finally, the Chamber will decide how much time goes for counsel and how much time goes for the accused --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know Your Honour doesn't want me to repeat the point I've already made, but it is impossible to separate these points. I should say straight away, there's no difficulty of communication between Mr. Krajisnik and me, provided we get physical access, of course, which is subject to all sorts of constraints. But there isn't a difficulty about that. Not surprising we don't always agree about everything. The -- Your Honour, the -- it really follows from what Your Honour is inviting me to do. What I can do and what I do do with Mr. Krajisnik, as far as I possibly can, is I indicate to Mr. Krajisnik as best I can how long I expect I would take as his counsel with my cross-examination doing my duty, having the conduct of this case as his counsel. That gives Mr. Krajisnik information from which he can work. But, Your Honour, I will, please, make it absolutely plain, I am not going to trade off any time of my cross-examination with Mr. Krajisnik under the direction of the Trial Chamber or not under the direction of the Trial Chamber because I have the conduct of this case, Your Honour. If the Trial Chamber chooses to allow Mr. Krajisnik, and it is your prerogative that under the status quo we are under at the moment, and I reserve all my rights and position in relation to that, Your Honour, but we live with the status quo while all these negotiations are going on. But if the Trial Chamber chooses to give Mr. Krajisnik time for cross-examination, so far as my conduct of the case is concerned, Your Honour, that really is nothing to do with me. I will not trade off my conduct of the case and my time for cross-examination in the way that Your Honour indicates. I will give the information and I will help Mr. Krajisnik in that way. He can work from that. The Trial Chamber know where we are on that, and we can proceed accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the matter. We adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 30th day of June, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
